title: Dress, lighting and owners at the Panama
summary: Performers wore their own street clothes with high collars, no one tried to look sexy, lighting was dim, and Izzy Levine and Izzy Shore owned the plain place.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Well, we all used to wear pretty nice clothes.
Yes, we wore street clothes. Because I know I featured smart blouses. And all my blouses had high collars.
So you wore your own clothes.
Everybody wore their own clothes. Anybody that wanted to put on an evening dress put it on, but at that time we didn't bother so much about evening clothes.
But did girls try to look sexy and --
No. They didn't bother. They didn't need to bother about sex, because those fellows weren't thinking about that, anyhow.

All they wanted was for those women to make money, you know, and that's all. So we didn't bother about being sexy, although we wanted to be smartly dressed, but we didn't do it especially to show our -- our bodies, you know.
Was there much light in these places?
Were there candles on the tables?
No. No. Not too much. I don't remember anything like that in the Panama. I don't remember anything like that.
No. You haven't gotten to the chandeliers, yet. The chandeliers are further up.
Uh-huh. No, we haven't gotten to the --
Just sort of a fairly lowdown --
It wasn't what you'd call lowdown. It was just a plain, ordinary place where Izzy Levine and them wanted to make money, and they made it.
Izzy Shore. They had the Panama.
Izzy Levine. Izzy Levine. You haven't got him down there, have you?
Izzy Levine and Izzy Shore. They had the Panama. Then, after the Panama I'm sure I went next door to the De Luxe.
